scenes.heading: Ageing and cell death
scenes.sub: Why your cells are built to die on cue
scenes.say: Your fingers separated before you were born because the cells between them died on cue. So how do cells die, why do they age, and how does cancer escape both limits?

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Hard rubbish night: the couch is put out neatly and taken away
scenes.science: Apoptosis: the cell packs itself up and phagocytes remove it
scenes.breaks: Apoptosis is something the cell actively does using ATP, and the 'eat me' signal is moved to the outer membrane face, not added.
scenes.say: Think of hard rubbish night: the old couch goes out neatly and is taken away with no mess. That's apoptosis. The cell packs itself up, shows an eat me signal, and phagocytes remove it. Necrosis is a wheelie bin split open in the street: everything spills, causing inflammation.

scenes.heading: Apoptosis vs necrosis
scenes.say: Ask yourself: shrink and pack, or swell and burst? Apoptosis is programmed and needs ATP. The cell shrinks and is packaged up, with no inflammation. Necrosis follows severe injury, like loss of blood supply. The cell swells, bursts, and triggers inflammation.

scenes.heading: The caspase pathways
scenes.say: Apoptosis is carried out by caspases, protein-cutting enzymes. Eight from outside, nine from inside, both meet at three. A death receptor activates caspase eight. Cytochrome c released from mitochondria activates caspase nine. Both switch on caspase three, and the cascade becomes irreversible.

scenes.heading: Telomeres and senescence
points: Telomeres: TTAGGG repeats at chromosome ends
End-replication problem: they shorten each copy
scenes.say: Telomeres are repeated DNA at chromosome ends, like the plastic tips on shoelaces. Because of the end-replication problem, they shorten each time DNA is copied. When critically short, the cell enters senescence: alive, but permanently stopped dividing. Telomerase can add the repeats back.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Telomeres are 9 kb at doubling 10 and 6 kb at doubling 40. Cells senesce at about 4 kb. How many more doublings?
scenes.say: Telomeres drop from nine to six kilobases over thirty doublings. That's one hundred base pairs per doubling. Senescence is at about four kilobases, so two thousand base pairs are left. Divide by one hundred: about twenty more doublings.
scenes.caption: Telomeres drop from 9 to 6 kb over 30 doublings. That's 100 bp per doubling. Senescence is at about 4 kb, so 2000 bp are left. Divide by 100: about 20 more doublings.

scenes.heading: Cancer: accelerator and brakes
scenes.say: Cancer is loss of control. An oncogene is a stuck accelerator: one mutated copy is enough. A tumour suppressor like T P fifty-three is the brakes, and usually both copies must be lost. Cancer cells also evade apoptosis and switch telomerase back on.
scenes.caption: Cancer is loss of control. An oncogene is a stuck accelerator: one mutated copy is enough. A tumour suppressor like TP53 is the brakes, and usually both copies must be lost. Cancer cells also evade apoptosis and switch telomerase back on.

points: Apoptosis: shrink and pack, no inflammation
Cancer: oncogenes on, tumour suppressors off
scenes.say: Recap. Apoptosis is tidy, necrosis is messy. Caspase eight outside, nine inside, both meet at three. Short telomeres trigger senescence. Cancer comes from oncogenes on and tumour suppressors lost. Now try the practice questions!
